The notebooks below accompany Unit 2. They are ordinary Jupyter
notebooks and need only `numpy` (plus `matplotlib` for the plots); open
them in JupyterLab, VS Code, or any notebook environment.

## Inventory control with a stochastic demand

The inventory control problem of Unit 1, now with the demand random
rather than known, which is what forces the *stochastic* dynamic
programming algorithm. The stock still evolves as
$x_{k+1}=\max\{x_k+u_k-d_k,0\}$, but the recursion now minimizes an
expected cost, averaging the cost-to-go over the demand distribution at
each stage. A good first notebook for seeing what changes, and what does
not, when expectations enter the DP recursion.

[Download `A_2_StochInventoryControl.ipynb`](A_2_StochInventoryControl.ipynb){download="A_2_StochInventoryControl.ipynb"}

## Robot path planning: deterministic vs. stochastic

A robot must cross an environment with obstacles from left to right in
minimum time. The same problem is solved twice -- once assuming the
robot's moves are executed exactly, and once assuming each commanded move
succeeds only with some probability -- so that the deterministic and
stochastic policies can be compared directly. This is the example behind
the point, made in the notes, that planning as though the world were
deterministic and then simply replanning is not the same as accounting
for the uncertainty in the first place.

[Download `A_2_RobotPlanningStochastic.ipynb`](A_2_RobotPlanningStochastic.ipynb){download="A_2_RobotPlanningStochastic.ipynb"}

## Temperature control: why a thermostat switches rarely

A thermostat does not act at every time step, unlike most controllers --
it switches the heating on or off only when the temperature has drifted
far enough, which reduces wear on the equipment. This notebook shows that
such a switching rule is not merely a practical convenience but is
actually *optimal* for a simple stochastic model of the temperature
dynamics, recovering the familiar dead-band behaviour from the stochastic
dynamic programming algorithm.

[Download `A_2_K_TempControl.ipynb`](A_2_K_TempControl.ipynb){download="A_2_K_TempControl.ipynb"}

## Stochastic dynamic programming in Pac-Man's grid world

Pac-Man as a pursuit-evasion game: a ghost must chase Pac-Man across a
grid of 77 cells, where each may move to an adjacent cell or stay put at
every step. The notebook computes a policy for the ghost using stochastic
dynamic programming, with Pac-Man's moves treated as the disturbance. It
is the largest of the Unit 2 examples and gives a concrete feel for how
quickly the state space grows once the state has to describe *both*
players' positions.

[Download `A_2_A_Stochastic_DP_policy_pacman.ipynb`](A_2_A_Stochastic_DP_policy_pacman.ipynb){download="A_2_A_Stochastic_DP_policy_pacman.ipynb"}

## The buzz wire challenge

An open-ended assignment rather than a worked example. In the buzz wire
game a metal loop must be guided along a bent wire from one end to the
other without touching it; here the loop is held by a robot arm, and the
task is to find a strategy that traverses the wire as fast as possible.
The loop's configuration is its centre position $(p_x,p_y)$ together with
an orientation angle $\theta$, and both a deterministic model and a
stochastic one -- in which disturbances knock the position off the
commanded cell -- are set up, so the deterministic and stochastic dynamic
programming algorithms can be compared on a problem with a genuinely
three-dimensional state.

[Download `BuzwireChallenge.ipynb`](BuzwireChallenge.ipynb){download="BuzwireChallenge.ipynb"}
